questions.prompt: What is the Big-O running time of reading an array element by its index?

options.misconception: Confusing array indexing with binary search splitting.
Assuming finding an array element requires scanning from the beginning.
Confusing standard array lookup with comparison-based sorting complexity.

questions.explanation: Reading by index is constant time, O(1), because the work does not depend on how big the array is. Your notes use it as the classic O(1) example.

questions.prompt: An algorithm runs an O(n) loop and then, separately, an O(n²) loop. What is its overall running time?

options.misconception: Multiplying the running times of sequential loops instead of adding them.
Ignoring the dominant term and picking the smaller loop complexity.
Not dropping constants and lower-order terms from the total.

questions.explanation: Steps that run one after another add together, and the larger term dominates. O(n) + O(n²) simplifies to O(n²). Costs only multiply when one loop is nested inside the other.

questions.prompt: Which statement about Big-O notation is NOT true?

options.text: It ignores constant factors and lower-order terms
options.misconception: Thinking Big-O includes exact constants and lower-order terms.

options.text: An algorithm taking 3n + 7 steps is O(n)
options.misconception: Thinking 3n + 7 can't simplify to O(n).

options.text: An O(n) algorithm is faster than an O(n²) algorithm on every input size
It can describe memory use as well as running time
options.misconception: Believing asymptotic analysis applies exclusively to time and never space.

questions.explanation: Big-O describes how cost grows and deliberately drops constant factors, so it says nothing about which algorithm wins on every input. A small input with big constants can favor the O(n²) algorithm. The other three statements come straight from your notes.

questions.prompt: Binary search on a sorted array runs in O(log n) time because it halves the search range at each step.

options.misconception: Thinking binary search requires scanning every element linearly.

questions.explanation: Cutting the problem by a constant fraction each step is what makes an algorithm logarithmic, and binary search halves the range every time. So this statement is true.

questions.prompt: Why can an array read any element by its index in O(1) time?

options.text: It searches from both ends at once
options.misconception: Confusing array indexing with two-pointer search algorithms.

options.text: Elements sit in one contiguous block, so the address is computed directly
Each element stores a pointer to the next one
options.misconception: Confusing contiguous arrays with linked list pointer structures.

options.text: The array is always kept in sorted order
options.misconception: Assuming constant time access relies on the array being sorted.

questions.explanation: Because every element is the same size and stored contiguously, element i lives at the start address plus i times the element size. One calculation finds it, no matter how long the array is.

questions.prompt: What does a dynamic array do when you append to it while it is full?
questions.answer: It allocates a larger array, typically double the capacity, and copies every element over.
questions.explanation: A dynamic array grows by allocating a bigger underlying array, usually twice the capacity, and copying the elements across. That one append costs O(n), but it happens rarely.

questions.prompt: Appending to a dynamic array is called "amortized O(1)". What does that mean?

options.text: Every single append takes constant time
options.misconception: Believing dynamic arrays never need resizing and copying steps.

options.text: Averaged over a long sequence of appends, the cost per append is constant, even though an occasional append costs O(n)
Appending is O(1) only while the array is empty
options.misconception: Thinking amortized means a special case, not an average over many appends.

options.text: Appends are O(1) on random input but O(n²) in the worst case
options.misconception: Confusing amortized algorithmic complexity with average-case input distributions.

questions.explanation: Amortized analysis averages cost over a worst-case sequence. Doubling makes the expensive copies rare enough that total work stays proportional to the number of appends. It does not promise every append is fast.

questions.prompt: Inserting an element into the middle of an array takes O(1) time because only one slot changes.

options.misconception: Forgetting that inserting into an array middle requires shifting all subsequent elements.

questions.explanation: Inserting in the middle means shifting every later element one position over, which is O(n) in the worst case. That shifting is the main cost of contiguous storage.

questions.prompt: In a singly linked list, what does each node store?

options.text: A value and its index in the list
options.misconception: Assuming linked list nodes keep track of their own index numbers.

options.text: Only a pointer to the head
options.misconception: Confusing individual node contents with the entire linked list structure.

options.text: A value and a pointer to the next node
A value and pointers to two children
options.misconception: Confusing singly linked list nodes with binary tree nodes.

questions.explanation: Each node in a singly linked list holds its value plus a pointer to the next node, and the last node points to null. Two child pointers would make it a binary tree instead.

questions.prompt: Which operation is O(1) on a singly linked list that keeps only a head pointer?

options.text: Inserting a new node at the head
Appending a node at the end
options.misconception: Assuming a head-only linked list can append at the end in O(1) without a tail pointer.

options.text: Finding the element at position i
options.misconception: Believing linked lists support direct index-based access like arrays.
Assuming traversing to the end of a singly linked list is instantaneous.

questions.explanation: Inserting at the head only changes two pointers: the new node points to the old head, and the head points to the new node. The other options all require walking the list, which is O(n).

questions.prompt: You have a reference to a node in a singly linked list and want to delete it. What else do you need?

options.misconception: Confusing the tail pointer with the predecessor node needed for deletion.
Assuming numerical indices are used to locate and delete nodes in a linked list.
Forgetting that singly linked nodes lack backward pointers to their predecessors.

options.text: A reference to the node before it

questions.explanation: Deleting a node means updating its predecessor's next pointer, and a singly linked list cannot walk backward to find it. A doubly linked list stores that previous pointer, which is why deletion there is O(1) from the node alone.

questions.prompt: Linked lists usually traverse faster than arrays in practice because their nodes can live anywhere in memory.

options.misconception: Confusing memory allocation flexibility with fast CPU cache locality during traversal.

questions.explanation: Scattered nodes actually hurt: linked lists have poor cache locality, so traversal is usually slower than an array even though both are O(n). Arrays win because neighbors sit next to each other.

questions.prompt: What order does a stack follow when removing elements?
questions.answer: Last-In, First-Out (LIFO): the most recently added element is removed first.
questions.explanation: A stack is Last-In, First-Out: the most recently pushed element is the first one popped. FIFO describes a queue.

questions.prompt: Which data structure does breadth-first search use?

options.misconception: Confusing FIFO queue traversal with LIFO stack traversal.
Confusing graph traversal structures with associative lookup tables.
Confusing graph search frontiers with hierarchical tree structures.

questions.explanation: Breadth-first search uses a queue so that items are processed in the order they were discovered. Your notes pair stacks with depth-first search instead.

questions.prompt: Why is a plain array that dequeues from index 0 a poor way to build a queue?

options.misconception: Assuming arrays enforce uniqueness constraints like sets.
Guessing a log-time cost instead of the O(n) shift on every dequeue.

options.text: Every dequeue shifts all remaining elements, costing O(n)
Arrays can only be read from the end
options.misconception: Thinking arrays restrict reads exclusively to their ending boundary.

questions.explanation: Removing index 0 forces every remaining element to shift forward, so each dequeue is O(n). A circular buffer avoids this by wrapping its front and back indices around, giving O(1) operations.

questions.prompt: A program pushes 1, 2, 3 onto an empty stack, pops twice, pushes 4 and 5, then pops once. What does peek return?

options.misconception: Reading the bottom of the stack instead of the top.
Forgetting that the two pops removed 3 and then 2.
Forgetting that the final pop removed 5.

questions.explanation: Trace it: [1, 2, 3], two pops leave [1], pushing gives [1, 4, 5], and one pop leaves [1, 4]. Peek shows the top without removing it, which is 4.

questions.prompt: In a hash table, what is a collision?
questions.answer: When two different keys hash to the same index.
questions.explanation: A collision is when two different keys map to the same bucket index. Collisions are unavoidable, which is why every hash table needs a strategy such as chaining or open addressing.

questions.prompt: How does separate chaining handle collisions?

options.text: Each bucket holds a list of all entries that hashed to it
It probes the next slots until it finds an empty one
options.misconception: Confusing separate chaining with open addressing collision resolution.
Assuming hash tables drop colliding keys instead of storing them.
Confusing collision handling strategies with load factor resizing triggers.

questions.explanation: With separate chaining, each bucket keeps a list of every entry that hashed there, and lookup searches that one list. Probing for an empty slot is open addressing, the other strategy.

questions.prompt: A hash table has 16 buckets, holds 12 entries, and resizes when its load factor passes 0.75. What happens when one more entry is inserted?

options.text: The insert is rejected because 0.75 is the maximum load
options.misconception: Believing load factor limits prevent further insertions instead of triggering a resize.

options.text: The load factor stays at 0.75 because buckets are reused
options.misconception: Assuming the load factor remains static when capacity is not explicitly updated.

options.text: Only the bucket that collided gets bigger
options.misconception: Thinking hash table resizing only expands individual buckets rather than reallocating the array.

options.text: The load factor rises to about 0.81, so the table grows and rehashes every entry

questions.explanation: Load factor is entries divided by buckets: 13 / 16 ≈ 0.81, which passes the 0.75 threshold. The table allocates a larger bucket array and rehashes every entry, an O(n) step that is amortized O(1) per insert.

questions.prompt: A hash table makes it easy to list all of its keys in sorted order.

options.misconception: Confusing unordered hash table buckets with ordered search tree structures.

questions.explanation: Hash tables scatter keys across buckets and don't keep them in order, so sorted output takes extra work. Keeping keys in order is one of the things binary search trees do well.

questions.prompt: In a binary search tree, where are the keys smaller than a node's key stored?

options.misconception: Mixing up the left and right subtree ordering rules in a BST.
Confusing subtree distribution with root node placement.
Assuming data values are restricted to leaf nodes in a binary search tree.

questions.explanation: The BST rule puts every smaller key in the left subtree and every larger key in the right subtree. It applies to whole subtrees, not just a node's immediate children.

questions.prompt: Which traversal visits a binary search tree's keys in sorted order?
questions.answer: In-order traversal: left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree.
questions.explanation: An in-order traversal visits the left subtree, then the node, then the right subtree. On a BST that matches the ordering rule, so the keys come out sorted.

questions.prompt: The keys 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 are inserted in that order into a plain BST with no self-balancing. What results?

options.text: A list-like tree where each node is a right child, so searches take O(n)
A balanced tree with 30 at the root
options.misconception: Assuming plain BSTs automatically self-balance upon insertion.

options.text: A tree where every node is a left child
options.misconception: Mixing up which side larger keys go to in a BST.

options.text: A tree that rotates itself to keep O(log n) height
options.misconception: Thinking a plain BST rebalances itself like an AVL or red-black tree.

questions.explanation: Each new key is larger than everything before it, so it always goes right, and the tree degenerates into a chain. Its height becomes n, so operations slow to O(n). Self-balancing trees like AVL and red-black trees prevent this with rotations.

questions.prompt: Search, insert, and delete in a balanced binary search tree run in O(log n) time.

options.misconception: Confusing unbalanced BST worst-case linear time with balanced tree guarantees.

questions.explanation: BST operations take O(h) time, and a balanced tree with n nodes has height about log n, so this statement is true. That is why self-balancing trees work hard to stay balanced.
